title: Syntax
summary: The shape a program has to have before Python will run it at all.
refresher: **Syntax** is the set of rules your code has to follow before Python will run it. `print("Hi")` needs the parentheses, and the text inside needs matching quotes. A `#` starts a **comment**, which Python ignores. Lines that end in a colon start a **block**, and the lines belonging to that block are indented underneath. In Python, **indentation** is not decoration. It is how you say which lines go together.
refresher_code:
# a comment, ignored by Python
name = "Ada"
if name == "Ada":
    print("Hello, Ada")

output-01.title: Numbers add before they print
output-01.body: This checks whether the values are numbers or text. Number values use `+` for arithmetic before output happens.
output-01.notice: Evaluate the expression first, then decide what the output instruction shows.
output-01.mistake: Do not join digits like text unless quotes make them strings.

output-02.title: A variable name stands in for its value
output-02.body: The output line uses the stored value, not the variable name as literal text.
output-02.notice: Read the assignment first so the later output line has the value in place.
output-02.mistake: Do not choose an answer that prints the name itself when the code uses the variable.

output-03.title: Text plus text joins
output-03.body: When both sides are strings, `+` makes one longer string instead of doing arithmetic.
output-03.notice: Quotes are the clue that the values are text.
output-03.mistake: Do not add quoted digits as numbers unless the code converts them first.

output-04.title: Integer division keeps a whole result
output-04.body: This question tests the division rule for whole-number output in the selected language.
output-04.notice: Check whether the code asks for decimal division or a whole-number result.
output-04.mistake: Do not round up. Whole-number division keeps the complete groups.

output-05.title: Printing needs the exact output call
output-05.body: Type-in output questions care about the statement shape and the exact text being shown.
output-05.notice: Match the print/output function and include quotes around text.
output-05.mistake: Do not type only the word being printed when the question asks for a statement.

syntax-delimiter-01.title: Open delimiters need partners
syntax-delimiter-01.body: Brackets, parentheses, and quotes create a shape the parser must be able to close.
syntax-delimiter-01.notice: When code stops before running, scan for the opening symbol that never got closed.
syntax-delimiter-01.mistake: Do not debug the logic until the code can be parsed.

syntax-comment-01.title: Comments are skipped
syntax-comment-01.body: A comment can look like code, but the language ignores it when the program runs.
syntax-comment-01.notice: Only non-commented output statements affect what appears.
syntax-comment-01.mistake: Do not count a commented-out line as a printed line.

syntax-case-01.title: Names are case-sensitive
syntax-case-01.body: Capitalization can create a different name. Built-in words and user names must match exactly.
syntax-case-01.notice: If a familiar name fails, compare every letter including case.
syntax-case-01.mistake: Do not assume `Print` and `print` are the same spelling to the language.

syntax-line-break-01.title: Escapes can create invisible characters
syntax-line-break-01.body: Some characters inside strings describe formatting, such as moving output to the next line.
syntax-line-break-01.notice: Read escape sequences as one special character, not as ordinary letters.
syntax-line-break-01.mistake: Do not include the backslash text literally when the code asks for output.

syntax-block-01.title: Block headers need block syntax
syntax-block-01.body: A decision or loop header must clearly mark that a controlled body is coming next.
syntax-block-01.notice: Check the small symbol at the end of the header and the shape of the body below it.
syntax-block-01.mistake: Do not focus only on the condition and miss the punctuation that opens the block.

sections.title: Print one line of text
sections.summary: Start with the smallest runnable Python line: a print call with matching parentheses and quotes.

blocks.body: Every language has rules about how you are allowed to arrange things. English wants a subject and a verb. Python wants parentheses in certain places, quotes around text, and lines lined up in a certain way. Those rules are called **syntax**. Get them right and your program runs. Get one of them wrong and Python stops before it runs a single line. A **syntax error** is not the computer disagreeing with your idea. It is the computer saying it could not read the sentence at all. Your logic might be perfect. Python never got far enough to find out.

blocks.caption: The smallest useful program. `print` is the **instruction**, the parentheses hold what you want shown, and the quotes mark where the text starts and stops.

blocks.body: Each of those three pieces is doing a job. Without the parentheses, Python sees the word `print` and has nothing to **print**. Without the quotes, it reads `Hello` as the name of a **variable** and looks for one you never made. The punctuation is not there to look official. It is there to tell Python which parts are instructions and which parts are just text.

blocks.title: Quotes come in pairs
blocks.body: A **string** is text with quotes around both ends. Single quotes and double quotes both work, so `'hi'` and `"hi"` are the same to Python. What matters is that you close with the same kind you opened with. If you need an apostrophe inside your text, open with double quotes: `"it's fine"`.

blocks.caption: Python reads left to right looking for the closing quote, and when the line ends without one it stops right there. The message says the **string** was never terminated, and the little arrow underneath points at the quote that started it. Read the arrow. It is usually aiming straight at the problem.
blocks.wrong:
print("Hello)
# the quote after Hello
# was never closed
blocks.right:
print("Hello")
# opened with ", closed with "
# and the parenthesis closed too

sections.title: Comments and skipped lines
sections.summary: See how # turns code-looking text into **comments** Python ignores.

blocks.body: Anything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Python skips it entirely. Comments are for the humans reading your code later, and one of those humans is you in three weeks, wondering what you meant.

blocks.caption: Proof that Python really does ignore comments. The first line looks like a sentence and the second ends with one, yet the only thing that runs is `print("Welcome")`.
blocks.code:
# Prints a greeting for the user.
print("Welcome")  # you can also comment at the end of a line

choices: Nothing, it is all commented out
blocks.why: The `#` at the start of the first and third lines turns them into comments, so Python never runs them. Only the middle line is real code. If you picked "first, second, third", you read the lines as code because they look like code, which is a fair mistake. Python does not care what a commented line looks like. It stops reading at the `#` and moves on.

sections.title: Blocks, colons, and indentation
sections.summary: Learn how Python uses **colons** and **leading spaces** to decide which lines belong together.

blocks.body: Now the part that makes Python different from most other languages: **leading spaces** carry meaning. Some lines end with a **colon**, which says "a block is coming". The lines that belong to that block are indented underneath it. That is how you tell Python where the block starts and where it ends. So two lines in the same block need the same amount of space in front of them. Four spaces on one line and two on the next will stop the program. On your screen those two lines look almost identical. To Python they are not.

blocks.caption: The **colon** opens the block and the **four spaces** put a line inside it. The last line is not indented, so it sits outside the `if` and runs no matter what.
blocks.code:
score = 90

if score > 80:
    print("Nice work")
    print("Keep it up")

print("Done")
blocks.output:
Nice work
Keep it up
Done

blocks.title: The forgotten colon
blocks.body: Anything that opens a block needs a colon at the end of the line: `if`, `else`, `for`, `while`, `def`. Leave it off and Python reports a **syntax error** on that line or the next one. Experienced programmers still do this, because the colon is the easiest character in the language to skip over. When an error points at a line with `if` or `for` on it, check the end of the line first.

blocks.prompt: This code was meant to greet the user and then say goodbye. What is wrong with it?
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
if name == "Ada"
    print("Hello, Ada")
print("Goodbye")
choices: The `if` line is missing its colon
Nothing is wrong, it prints both lines
blocks.why: The `if` line opens a block, so it has to end with a colon. Without it the **file** never runs, and neither line prints. If you picked the indentation, that is a very reasonable guess, and plenty of people make it. Indentation is the thing Python is famous for, so it is the first place your eye goes. Here it happens to be fine: `print("Hello, Ada")` is correctly inside the `if`, and `print("Goodbye")` is correctly outside it so it runs either way.

sections.title: Read syntax errors like clues
sections.summary: Use the **error message** and a short checklist before rereading the whole file.

blocks.title: The error message is trying to help you
blocks.body: A **syntax error** tells you the line, and usually draws an arrow at the exact character that confused Python. Beginners often skim past all of it and start rereading the whole **file**. Read it instead. `expected ':'` means a colon is missing. `'(' was never closed` means a parenthesis is still open. `unterminated string literal` means a quote never got its partner. The message is naming your bug out loud.

blocks.title: A checklist for your first syntax errors
items: Every opening quote has a matching closing quote of the same kind
Every opening parenthesis has a closing one, including the one that closes `print(`
Every line that starts a block ends with a colon
Everything inside a block is indented, and indented by the same amount
Four spaces per level is the Python convention, and picking one style and sticking to it matters more than which style you pick
When you get a **syntax error**, read the arrow and the message before you change anything
